lessons.title: First look
lessons.blurb: Pick a source, orbit the camera, turn up Z Push, and make your first patch.

chapters.text: This is Rutt Etra Web, a browser recreation of the 1973 Rutt Etra scan processor, an analog video synthesizer.
No camera needed for this tour. Click Pattern, and the built-in pattern generator becomes the picture.
The image is drawn as horizontal scan lines. Brighter areas push the lines toward you, so the picture becomes a landscape.
Drag in the render window to orbit the virtual camera around it.
The Controls panel on the left holds every parameter. Type in the search box to find one. Here, Z Push, the depth of the raster.
Drag a knob up to turn it up. More push, deeper relief.
The Patch Bay on the right is the same instrument, laid out as a hardware faceplate. Maximize it to see every jack.
Right-click empty space to add a node. We will add an LFO, a slow oscillator.
Drag from the LFO's output jack onto Z Push's input. The cable is the patch.
Restore the window, and the raster now breathes on its own.
Pick a source, shape it, and patch movement into it. Next, we will learn our way around the windows.

lessons.title: Windows, tabs and layouts
lessons.blurb: Switch tabs, maximize a window, try layout presets, and change the panel skin.

chapters.text: The screen is four windows: left, center, right, and bottom. Each one holds tabs, like a desktop editor.
The tab strip names what each window shows. Here: the Controls, the Renderer, the Patch Bay, and the Timeline.
The arrow button in a window's corner maximizes it. Click it again to restore.
The minus button collapses a window down to just its tab strip. Click the strip, or the same button, to bring it back.
The Window menu has layout presets. Tall stacks everything into one column.
Default brings back the four-window layout.
Under View, pick a skin. CRT is flat and compact. Hardware turns sliders into knobs. Rack, the default, adds patch cables.
Control plus and Control minus change the text size. Control zero resets it.
Rearrange freely. Reset Layout, in the Window menu, always brings you home. Next: sources.

lessons.title: Sources
lessons.blurb: Pattern Generator kinds, and loading a video file as the picture.

chapters.text: Every picture starts with a source. You can pick one on the start screen, or any time in the Video Source A section of the Controls.
Open the Synth tab. Source is near the top.
The Pattern Generator makes pictures with no camera at all. Change its Kind to try another pattern. Lissajous.
Spiral. And Worley cells. Each kind brings its own controls, just below.
To use your own footage, choose a video file. Webcam, screen capture, and stream URLs work the same way.
The pattern was covering the whole picture, so loading a video switched it off. This is the video alone.
Turn the pattern back on, and set Blend to Screen. Now both show through.
Any source can feed the raster. Next, we will find our way around the Controls panel.

lessons.title: On your phone
lessons.blurb: The camera-style layout: pick a camera, swipe a look, take a photo, record a clip, and open the controls.

chapters.text: On a phone, Rutt Etra Web turns into a camera. The picture fills the screen, and the controls float over it.
Pick a source. Webcam is the front camera on a phone, so this is a selfie. You can also use the back camera, a video from your library, or the pattern with no camera at all.
Swipe the looks along the bottom, and tap one. Each look is a whole color and feel, applied in one tap.
Drag on the picture to orbit around it.
The flip button swaps between the front and back camera.
In Photo mode, the shutter saves a picture. On a phone, it opens your share sheet, so you can send it straight to a friend.
Switch to Video, and the shutter records. Tap it again to stop, and the clip is saved, with a Share button.
The tabs open the real controls. Source starts with the same four choices: front camera, back camera, your library, or the pattern.
Shape holds the scan processor: size, position, depth and rotation. Drag any bar to change it, and watch the picture behind the sheet.
More has presets, recording options, sharing, and the manual.
Turn the phone sideways, and the shutter moves to the edge. The Patch Bay and Timeline are on the desktop. Everything you save opens in either place.

lessons.title: Finding your way around
lessons.blurb: Tabs, sections, search, knobs, ranges, and the ⓘ help.

chapters.text: The Controls panel holds every parameter, in three tabs. Synth shapes the picture.
I O connects MIDI, audio, OSC, and control voltage. Help holds the manual. Back to Synth.
Each tab is a stack of sections. Click a header to fold a section open or closed.
To find anything fast, press slash, or click the search box, and type. Bloom.
Drag a knob up or down to change it. Hold Shift for fine control. Double-click to reset it.
The small arrow by a knob opens its menu: type an exact value, widen the knob's range, or reset.
The i button on a section header explains it, and draws what is patched into it right now.
Press Escape in the search box to clear it, and everything folds back the way it was.
Next, we will use these controls to shape the raster itself.

lessons.title: Shaping the raster
lessons.blurb: Size, depth, rotation and luminance — the scan processor itself.

chapters.text: The Display Control Unit is the scan processor itself. It decides where every line is drawn.
H Size and V Size stretch the raster. H Position and V Position slide it around.
Z Push is depth: how far bright areas lift toward you. Z Bias moves the whole sheet forward or back.
Rotation turns the raster in its own plane.
V Spin turns it around its vertical axis.
Threshold hides the darkest parts of the picture, so only the brighter areas draw.
Intensity sets the brightness of the beam. Focus softens or sharpens it.
Double-click any knob to put it back. Next: color, glow, and presets.

lessons.title: Color, glow and presets
lessons.blurb: Bloom, feedback, the virtual camera, and one-click presets.

chapters.text: Color and Post FX change how the beam looks on screen, after the scan processor has drawn it.
Color Mode picks the phosphor. Amber, like an old terminal. Then back to green.
Bloom is the phosphor glow. Push the intensity for a hot, blown-out beam.
Burn-In Feedback leaves trails, like slow phosphor. Turn it on, and move the camera to see them.
In Virtual Camera, Field of View works like a zoom lens.
Presets apply a whole look at once. Heavy Bloom. Lissajous Scope. Classic 1974.
Mix and match, then save your own look in the Presets section. Next: modulation.

lessons.title: Modulation
lessons.blurb: A Classic modulation slot: a sine wave moving a parameter.

chapters.text: Modulation moves parameters for you, so the picture keeps changing on its own. Open the Modulation section.
Classic mode has four slots. Each is a function generator: a source, a target, and an amount.
Slot one's source is already a sine wave. Set its target to Z Push.
Switch the slot on.
Amount is how far it swings. Turn it up, and the raster starts to breathe.
Expand the slot for more. Rate sets how fast the wave cycles, in hertz.
This slot also appears in the Patch Bay as Function Generator one. Next: the Timeline.

lessons.title: Keyframes
lessons.blurb: Create a timeline, key a parameter at two bars, and play it back.

chapters.text: The Timeline, along the bottom, plays changes back over time, locked to the tempo.
Click the plus button to make a timeline. It is sixteen bars long, at one hundred twenty beats per minute.
Click the ruler to move the playhead. Bar one.
Every knob has a small diamond above it. Click Z Push's diamond to set a keyframe at the playhead.
Move to bar three, and turn Z Push up. Once a parameter has a lane, every change is keyed automatically.
The lane below draws the curve, in the same numbers as the knob.
Press Play. The depth rises from bar one to bar three, holds, and the timeline loops.
Key as many parameters as you like. Next: scenes, which capture a whole look at once.

lessons.title: Scenes
lessons.blurb: Snapshot whole looks as scenes and let the timeline move between them.

chapters.text: Scenes capture every setting at once. The timeline blends from one scene to the next.
Double-click the Scenes track near the start, to capture the current look.
Now change the look. Apply the Amber Terminal preset, and push the depth.
Double-click at bar four, to capture the second scene.
Rewind, and press Play. The picture travels from the first look to the second.
Right-click a scene marker to preview it, replace its snapshot, or change its easing.
Keyframes and scenes work together on one timeline. Next: the Patch Bay.

lessons.title: Reading the Patch Bay
lessons.blurb: The faceplate: sources, parameter cells, the ⓘ diagrams, zoom and pan, free layout, and why a cable will not connect.

chapters.text: The Patch Bay is the whole instrument, drawn as a hardware faceplate. Maximize it, and everything is in front of you at once.
Along the top is the Sources bus: every signal you can patch from. Waveforms, audio, beats, MIDI, and the joystick.
Every parameter gets a cell. An input jack on the left, a knob with its number, and an output jack on the right. Turn a knob here, and the same parameter moves in the Controls panel.
Each module has a small i button. It opens an info panel, with a diagram of everything patched into that module right now. As you add cables, the diagram follows.
Scroll to zoom the board toward your cursor, and drag empty background to pan. The hundred percent button puts it back.
Free breaks every module out, so you can arrange the board like a canvas. Tidy snaps them back into stacks. Dragging any module by its header does the same for just that one.
Cables run from an output into an input. Try something that cannot work, and the jack glows red and tells you why.
Next, the cables themselves.

lessons.title: Cables
lessons.blurb: Waveforms into a function generator, its output into a parameter; move and unplug.

chapters.text: The Patch Bay is the whole instrument as one hardware faceplate. Maximize it to see more.
Along the top, the Sources bus offers signals: waveforms, audio, beats, MIDI, and more. Every parameter has an input jack, a knob, and an output jack.
Cables run from an output to an input. Drag the triangle wave down onto Function Generator one, the same slot as in the Modulation panel. Near an edge, the board scrolls with you.
Now its output. Grab the output jack, and carry it up to H Size.
Restore the window. The raster now stretches in and out with the triangle wave.
Back in the bay, grab a cable by its input end to move it. Drop it on V Size.
Drop a cable in empty space to unplug it.
Cables and the Modulation panel are two views of one patch. Next: nodes.

lessons.title: Nodes and the Scope
lessons.blurb: Add nodes with a right-click, watch signals on a Scope, delete what you do not need.

chapters.text: Nodes are extra modules: oscillators, envelopes, logic, and more. Right-click empty board space to add one. An LFO.
Add a Scope beside it. A scope draws whatever signal passes through it.
Drag the LFO's output into the Scope's input. There's the wave.
The Scope passes its signal on. Patch its output into Z Push, and the raster follows the wave.
Turn the LFO's rate knob, and watch the trace speed up.
To remove a node, click its X and confirm. Its cables go with it.
Every node type is listed in the Node Catalog on the About page. Next: routing video.

lessons.title: Video routing
lessons.blurb: Composite a video file with the Pattern Generator and feed the renderer.

chapters.text: The Patch Bay also routes the picture itself. Video cables are magenta.
Load a video into Video Source A, with its File button.
Open its preview to check that it is playing.
Now patch the Pattern Generator's video output into Composite's B input.
Set the Composite blend to Screen, so both pictures show.
Finally, patch Composite's output into the Renderer's input.
Restore the window. The raster now carries both pictures at once.
Video Source B and Dual Raster patch the same way. From here, everything is one cable away.

lessons.title: Patch Bay power moves
lessons.blurb: One parameter driving another, Note nodes, the same patch in the Controls panel, and a window of its own.

chapters.text: A few moves turn the Patch Bay into an instrument. First: one parameter driving another.
Every parameter has an output jack as well as an input. Drag the output of Z Push onto the input of H Size. Now the width follows the depth, and a Param Out node carries the signal behind the scenes.
Right-click empty space, and add a Note. Type on it. Notes are labels that live in the patch, so you can explain what a patch is for.
Restore the window, and open Modulation in the Controls panel. The cable you just made is a row there. The Patch Bay and the Controls panel are two views of one patch.
For two displays, the pop-out button on a window sends it to a browser window of its own. It stays live, and the main window keeps working.
Save a preset or a project, and every cable and note goes with it. Open it later, here or on another machine, and it all comes back.
That is the Patch Bay. The next level up is the Graph engine.

lessons.title: Graph mode and the Library
lessons.blurb: Beginner view rows, Noise and Ramp sources, ready-made patches, and Both mode.

chapters.text: Classic mode gives you four fixed slots. Graph mode is a node engine with more than fifty node types. Switch the Modulation section to Graph.
Beginner view looks like the Classic slots, but each row is a real node with a binding. Click Add patch: an LFO into Z Push.
Change its source to Noise. White noise jitters the depth on every frame.
Point it at Rotation instead, and turn the amount up. Now the whole raster shivers.
Add a second row. A Ramp, sweeping H Size from narrow to wide, over and over.
The Library holds ready-made patches. Load Getting Started, a slow breathing depth with a note explaining it.
Both mode runs Classic slots and the graph together, so switching never throws your slots away.
Beginner view covers simple one-to-one patches. Next, the Advanced canvas, where nodes feed each other.

lessons.title: The Advanced canvas
lessons.blurb: Add nodes, wire them, edit them in the inspector, bind to the synth, and probe a signal.

chapters.text: Advanced view is the full node canvas. Maximize the Controls window to give it room. The palette on the left lists every node by category.
Click a palette item to add a node. An LFO. A Clock. And a Sample and Hold.
Drag nodes by their headers to lay the patch out, left to right.
Drag from an output dot to an input dot. The LFO into the Sample and Hold's input. The Clock's pulse into its trigger.
Click a node to edit it in the inspector. Speed the LFO up, so every sample lands somewhere new.
Bindings send a node to the synth. Add a binding from the Sample and Hold to Z Push.
Probe draws a live trace of any output. Stepped values: the classic sample and hold staircase.
Restore the window. The depth now jumps to a new random level on every beat.
Every node works this way: outputs to inputs, bindings to the synth. Next, two pictures at once with Dual Raster.

lessons.title: Dual Raster
lessons.blurb: A second raster with its own geometry, wipe and interleave modes, and its own picture from the Patch Bay.

chapters.text: Dual Raster draws a second, independent raster alongside the first, like the two-channel scan processors of the seventies. Here the source is a camera.
Open the Dual Raster section and switch on raster B.
Trace splits the frame between the two. Sweep it across: A on one side, B on the other.
Raster B has its own geometry. Push its depth the other way, and turn it.
Alternate lines interleaves them instead. Every other scan line belongs to B.
B still shows the camera. In the Patch Bay, give it a picture of its own: the Pattern Generator's output into Dual Raster's B input.
Then the Dual Raster's output into the Renderer.
Restore the window. The camera and the pattern now share one raster, line by line.
Each raster can take a camera, a file, a stream, a pattern, or a composite of two. Next, sound.

lessons.title: Audio-reactive
lessons.blurb: The Audio section, beat detector, spectrum displacement, and an audio-reactive graph patch.

chapters.text: Everything here can react to sound. On the I O tab, the Audio section listens to a microphone, an audio file, or another tab.
Choose Microphone. A test tone stands in for a real mic here. Linear spacing spreads the bands evenly, and the spectrum shows each beep arrive.
Turn on the beat detector. Its light flashes on every hit, and Beat becomes a modulation source.
Spectrum to Z displacement lifts each scan line by its own frequency band. Turn up the amount.
Or patch sound anywhere. In Graph mode, the Library has an audio-reactive bloom patch. Load it, and the glow pumps with every beep.
Classic slots can use Audio, a single band, or Beat as their source, too.
Plug in a real mic, or load a song file, and the whole picture plays along. Next: the oscilloscope.

lessons.title: The Oscilloscope
lessons.blurb: Draw any signal as a trace and let the raster turn it into terrain.

chapters.text: The Pattern Generator has an Oscilloscope kind: it draws a signal as a glowing trace. Turn it on over the camera, set Kind to Oscilloscope, and Blend to Add.
A thin trace barely lifts the raster, so make it thick. Now it rides across the picture as a ridge.
Set the scope's source to Classic Slot, and its reference to one: modulation slot one.
Switch slot one on. Its sine wave is drawn live.
Change the waveform to a square wave, and the trace snaps between two levels.
Sweep sets how fast the trace crosses the screen. Persist sets how long it glows.
The scope can also draw audio, a graph node, any parameter, or the beat pulse.
A scope as a video source: any signal in the synth can become the picture. Next: deeper looks.

lessons.title: Render modes and Post FX
lessons.blurb: Wireframe and dot rasters, custom tint, shaped feedback, analog character, chroma, scanlines.

chapters.text: Beyond bloom and color, Geometry and Post FX change the whole character of the beam.
Geometry sets how the raster is drawn. Wireframe makes it a solid mesh. Dot Raster draws only the points.
Custom Tint picks any phosphor color you like. Magenta, for a start.
Burn-In Feedback leaves trails. Its shape can be a circle, so only the middle of the frame smears. Move the camera to paint with it.
Analog Character adds grain, dropouts and a rolling hum bar, like a tired old monitor.
Chromatic aberration splits the colors at the edges. Scanlines and a vignette finish the CRT look.
Each effect has its own on switch, and every slider can be modulated. Next: saving and sharing your work.

lessons.title: Save, record, share
lessons.blurb: User presets, project files, recording a clip, and live sharing with a link and QR code.

chapters.text: Three ways to keep your work: presets save a look, projects save everything, and recordings save the picture.
In Presets, name the current look and click Save Current. It joins your saved presets, ready to load later.
Try another look, then load yours back from the saved list.
Project, at the top of the Synth tab, saves the whole workspace: settings, presets, timelines and patches. Save As asks for a name, and the file downloads.
Record captures the output as a video file. Start, let it run, then Stop and Download.
Share broadcasts the output live. Start Broadcast gives you a link and a QR code; anyone who opens it watches in their browser.
WHIP output streams to OBS, MediaMTX or Cloudflare instead, for bigger audiences.
That covers the intermediate course. The advanced lessons start with deep patching.

lessons.title: Clocks, sequencers, envelopes
lessons.blurb: A tempo clock driving a step sequencer, a divided clock firing an ADSR envelope, probed live.

chapters.text: Clocks turn time into events. Add a Clock. It ticks in step with the tempo, which the Timeline sets.
Add a Sequencer, and patch the Clock's pulse into its clock input. Every tick advances one step.
Each step holds a value. Shape the pattern: a spike on step two, a dip on step four.
Bind the sequencer to Z Push, and the depth steps in rhythm.
Clock divide by N slows a clock down. Here it passes only every fourth tick.
Trigger to Gate stretches each tick into a gate. The ADSR envelope turns that gate into a swell and a slow fade.
Send the envelope to Bloom Intensity: the glow swells once a bar.
Probe the envelope to see its shape: attack, decay, sustain, release.
Restore the window. Stepped depth, and a breathing glow, both locked to the beat.
Change the tempo, and the whole patch follows. Next: feedback, and a little chaos.

lessons.title: Feedback and chaos
lessons.blurb: Resonant filtered noise, Param Out, a frame delay, and a patch that feeds on itself.

chapters.text: Nodes can feed each other, and they can feed back. Start with Noise: a new random value on every frame.
Raw noise is jittery. A resonant low-pass filter turns it into a slow, rubbery wobble.
Send the filtered noise to H Position, Rotation and Z Push. The raster drifts like it is underwater.
Param Out reads any parameter's live value back into the graph. This one reads Z Push.
Delay it by thirty frames, half a second, and scale it up.
Now close the loop: send the delayed copy back into Z Push. The depth chases its own echo. Keep the loop gain below one, or it runs away.
Probe the loop. No two cycles are quite the same.
Restore the window, and let it run.
Feedback is where the strange stuff lives. Keep the amounts small, and nudge. Next: the camera as a modulation source.

lessons.title: The camera as a source
lessons.blurb: Video Luma with a picked region, Video Motion through a Slew, and the motion-glitch patch.

chapters.text: The picture can drive the synth, too. Video nodes measure brightness, motion, color and edges in the live image.
Add Video Luma. It reports how bright a region of the frame is.
Drag on the thumbnail in the inspector to choose the region. Here, the moving shape in the middle.
Bind it to Z Push. Now the depth follows that part of the picture.
Video Motion measures how much the image is changing. Smooth it with a Slew, and send it to Bloom.
The Library has more: Motion-Triggered Glitch tears the raster whenever something moves.
Restore the window. The camera is now playing the synth.
Point a webcam at a dancer, a lava lamp, or your own hands. Next: MIDI and OSC.

lessons.title: MIDI and OSC
lessons.blurb: Connect a controller, learn a mapping, MIDI clock in and out, and OSC over the network.

chapters.text: The I O tab connects the synth to the outside world. First, MIDI. Click Connect MIDI, and pick your controller.
To map a knob, choose a target, click Learn, then move the control. Here, Z Push.
Now the controller plays the depth directly. Each binding has its own curve and range.
MIDI clock in sets the tempo from a drum machine or a DAW. The readout shows the incoming BPM. Clock Out sends the tempo the other way.
OSC works over the network, from TouchOSC, Max, or SuperCollider, through the small bridge in the tools folder. Enter the bridge address and connect.
Learn works the same way: choose H Size, click Learn, and send a message.
Every OSC message on that address now moves the parameter. Copy TouchOSC layout gives you a ready-made control surface.
MIDI and OSC sources also exist as graph nodes, for patching instead of mapping. Next: control voltage, gamepads and MCP.

lessons.title: CV, gamepads and MCP
lessons.blurb: Control voltage inputs, OSC CV, gamepads, and an AI assistant driving the synth over MCP.

chapters.text: Control voltage connects modular synthesizers. Through a DC-coupled audio interface, each input channel becomes a modulation source.
Pick the interface, choose how many channels, and start the CV reader. A test signal stands in for a real interface here.
Each channel shows its live voltage. Set its range, plus or minus five volts for Eurorack, its polarity and smoothing, and Calibrate to zero it.
No interface? A Raspberry Pi with an analog to digital converter can send CV as OSC instead. Add an OSC CV channel and give it an address.
Gamepads and HID controllers appear here, too. Every axis and button becomes a source.
MCP lets an AI assistant, like Claude, drive the synth through the bridge in the tools folder. Connect to the bridge.
Now the assistant is in control. It deepens the raster, widens it, turns it, and then builds a modulation patch from scratch.
Anything an assistant can set, it can also read back: parameters, patches, even a screenshot. Next: the outputs.

lessons.title: Outputs
lessons.blurb: Sonification and the Sonify node, CV Out to a modular, MIDI clock out, and the safety stack.

chapters.text: The synth can send signals out, too. Every output starts switched off and quiet, with a soft start and a limiter, so nothing surprises your speakers or your modular.
Sonification turns the picture into sound. A voice reads the raster: its brightness, motion and shape set pitch, loudness and filter.
Each voice parameter has a source and a curve. Pick Graph Node, and a Sonify node in the graph can play the voice directly.
Master volume starts at minus eighteen decibels. Test Tone checks your levels, and Sonification mutes itself whenever a microphone is listening, to avoid feedback.
CV Out sends control voltage to a modular through a DC-coupled interface. Add an output and choose its type: continuous CV, gate, trigger, clock, or one volt per octave pitch.
Its source can be a modulation slot, a graph node, any parameter, the Pattern Generator, MIDI notes, or the tempo clock.
And MIDI Clock Out, in the MIDI section, sends the tempo to drum machines and DAWs.
Inputs and outputs together make the synth one module in a bigger system. Next: stereo and 3D.

lessons.title: Stereo and 3D
lessons.blurb: Red-cyan anaglyph, side-by-side stereo recording, and WebXR headsets.

chapters.text: The raster is a real 3D object, so it can be shown in real 3D. Three ways: anaglyph, side-by-side stereo, and WebXR headsets.
Anaglyph is in the Virtual Camera section. Switch it on and grab some red and cyan glasses.
Eye Sep sets how far apart the two eyes are. More separation, more depth. Orbit the camera to feel it.
For VR players and YouTube, the Record section can capture side-by-side stereo, with an optional 3D metadata tag.
Preview stereo shows both eyes for three seconds, before you commit to a recording.
With a WebXR headset connected, the XR section puts you inside the raster, at tabletop, room or architectural scale.
Next: building a performance rig.

lessons.title: A performance rig
lessons.blurb: Layouts, HUD, shortcuts, performance profiles, output resolution, fly mode, timecode and popouts.

chapters.text: On stage you want the picture big and the controls close. The Performance layout maximizes the output.
Press H for the HUD: frame rate, source and render size. Press it again to hide it.
Back to the default layout. Bracket keys flip between the panel tabs, and slash jumps to the search box.
The Performance section trades quality for speed. Battery caps the frame rate and drops the heavy effects. Render Scale changes the internal resolution.
Virtual Camera sets a fixed output resolution, like full HD for a projector, letterboxed to fit.
Fly mode turns the camera into a free-flying ship: W A S D to move, the mouse to steer, Shift to boost.
For syncing with video, the Timeline can count in timecode, frames, or samples instead of bars.
And for two screens, Window, Pop Out Output sends the picture to its own window, ready to go fullscreen on a projector, while the controls stay on your laptop.
Last lesson: putting it all together.

lessons.title: Showcase: getting weird
lessons.blurb: Five strange setups: a feedback tunnel, interleaved worlds, resonant chaos, sound terrain, anaglyph Lissajous.

chapters.text: To finish, six setups built from everything in this course. None of them took more than a minute. Let's get weird.
One. A feedback tunnel. The camera, amber phosphor, circular burn-in with a long decay, and the camera slowly orbiting.
Every frame smears into the next, so the picture leaves a trail of itself.

Two. Interleaved worlds. Dual Raster, alternate lines, with raster B pushed the opposite way and turned. Two copies of the same camera, woven together. One pushes toward you, the other falls away, and every other scan line flips between them, so the picture seems to argue with itself. Orbit around it, and the two layers slide apart.
Three. Resonant chaos, loaded from a saved patch: filtered noise wobbling the rotation, and a feedback loop chasing the depth. Wireframe mode makes it a sculpture.
Four. Sound terrain. The microphone drives spectrum displacement, so every frequency band lifts its own scan lines. Magenta, with heavy bloom.

Five. The raster, turned inside out. One low frequency oscillator on horizontal linearity, another on vertical, and then we turn the amount up. The lines pinch, fold, and flip over themselves, and all of it is the same camera.
Six. A Lissajous figure, in red and cyan anaglyph, drifting in 3D. Put on the glasses.
That's the instrument. Now go make something nobody has seen before.
